content.text:
The discussion is not exposing a config-loading bug. It’s conflating two separate behaviors:

- Selected bootstrap roots already load active files such as `mise.dev.toml`; this is explicit in the loader and covered by tests. See [src/config/mod.rs](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/3e70/mise/src/config/mod.rs:1742) and [docs/bootstrap.md](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/3e70/mise/docs/bootstrap.md:409).
- Loading a file does not mean every section in it is composed into the parent bootstrap operation. Only dotfiles, files, directories, services, and Compose projects are composed. [Discussion #12987](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12987) is asking about the deliberately excluded surfaces from the earlier [#12120 answer](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12120).

Current coverage is:

| Surface | Existing behavior |
|---|---|
| Tasks | `[monorepo].config_roots` supplies the shared task namespace |
| Tools | `mise install --monorepo` / `mise ls --monorepo` aggregate them |
| Packages | Not composed across bootstrap roots |
| Repos | Not composed |
| Accounts | Not composed |
| Hooks | Not composed or executed |
| Non-composed bootstrap declarations | Inspectable with `mise bootstrap config-roots --json` |

The latter command was added in PR [#12770](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12770), following [Discussion #12756](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/12756). Its output includes the active environment-specific config and declaration provenance, but intentionally performs no convergence. See [docs/bootstrap.md](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/3e70/mise/docs/bootstrap.md:437).

My recommendation: don’t promise that `mise.<env>.toml` will “accommodate” the remaining sections. It already works, and changing the filename does not solve cross-root execution semantics. The defensible next feature would be explicit per-root fan-out for packages/repos/accounts/hooks—each root retaining its hierarchy and environment—rather than merging unrelated sibling maps into one config. That preserves hook lifecycle, package-manager ordering, and repository ownership boundaries.

A concise response would be:

> `mise.<env>.toml` files already load normally inside every selected `[bootstrap].config_roots` root, so environment selection and root composition are working independently. They don’t widen which sections are composed, though.
>
> Tasks and tools already have aggregate workflows through `[monorepo].config_roots` and `mise install --monorepo`. Packages, repos, accounts, and hooks remain per-root; `mise bootstrap config-roots --json` can now report which active root declares them.
>
> If we extend this further, I think it should be explicit fan-out execution per selected root rather than merging those sections. In particular, hooks need root-local lifecycle ordering, and packages/repos need conflict and ownership semantics.
>
> *AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: openai/GPT-5; version: unavailable.*

No repository changes appear necessary for this investigation.
i almost think i should never have shipped config\_roots

I think that instinct is justified—the name `config_roots` promises “load these configurations,” while the implementation means “extract a selected set of bootstrap resources from these configurations.” Discussion #12987 is the predictable result: users naturally expect every section to participate.

I wouldn’t expand it further. That turns bootstrap into a second monorepo/config-composition engine, with increasingly awkward semantics for precedence, tools, hooks, packages, and execution context.

I also wouldn’t immediately remove it. It solves a real resource-bundling use case and already has users. I’d contain it:

- Freeze composition at declarative, conflict-detectable resources.
- Explicitly reject the idea that variant filenames broaden composition.
- Treat tasks/tools through `[monorepo]`, and leave imperative bootstrap surfaces root-local.
- Consider renaming the concept to `[bootstrap].resource_roots` or `[bootstrap].includes`, with `config_roots` retained as a deprecated alias under the normal 12-month policy.

The mistake wasn’t necessarily shipping composition; it was exposing it as composition of entire “config roots.” A narrower name and contract can keep the useful part without accepting the architectural consequences implied by the current name.
i think we should've left bootstrap at global/system level

Yes—that is the cleaner boundary.

`[tools]`, `[env]`, and `[tasks]` describe a directory or project. `[bootstrap]` describes desired machine/user state: packages, accounts, services, repositories, dotfiles, and lifecycle hooks. Letting directory traversal influence that state makes the current working directory part of provisioning semantics, which is surprising and potentially dangerous.

`[bootstrap].config_roots` then became a workaround for making machine configuration modular inside a configuration system fundamentally organized around project ancestry. That’s why every additional surface needs bespoke rules.

I’d move toward this model:

- Bootstrap reads only global and system configuration.
- Project dependencies belong in `mise deps`; project tools remain in `[tools]`.
- A setup repository can become the global configuration source during adoption.
- Modular bootstrap configuration uses explicit includes/fragments rooted in that global configuration—not sibling “config roots.”
- Project-local `[bootstrap]` and `[bootstrap].config_roots` are deprecated, then removed under the normal compatibility schedule.

The useful idea worth preserving is modular machine configuration. The part to unwind is having bootstrap inherit from arbitrary project configuration and compose independently loaded project roots. That would give `mise bootstrap` one stable meaning regardless of where it is invoked.
let's hide it in the docs, mark it as deprecated immediately, say it needs more design thinking, put removal 6 months out, post a reply

I’ll narrow the public documentation, add an immediate runtime deprecation warning with a six-month removal date as requested, cover it with focused tests, and then reply on Discussion #12987 with the migration/design rationale.

-## Composing configuration roots
-
-`[bootstrap].config_roots` composes declarative resources from independent
-configuration roots into the current bootstrap operation:
-
-```toml
-[bootstrap]
-config_roots = ["bundles/*"]
-```
-
-Entries are relative to the declaring config root and may use single-level `*`
-globs. Each matched directory is loaded with the normal active configuration
-environments. Relative resource sources and template `config_root` values remain
-relative to the config that declared them. Variables declared by a selected root
-are available to that root's dotfile templates without leaking into sibling
-roots.
-
-Composition includes `[dotfiles]`, `[bootstrap.files]`,
-`[bootstrap.directories]`, `[bootstrap.services]`, and `[bootstrap.compose]`.
-Equivalent declarations are deduplicated. Different declarations for the same
-dotfile target, edit `(path, id)`, managed file, managed directory, service, or
-Compose project are errors that identify both declaring configs. Independent
-roots never acquire precedence from their order in `config_roots`.
-Same-target `symlink-each` declarations are the exception: their source trees
-compose when their leaf paths are disjoint, while overlapping leaves or
-file/directory collisions are reported with both declaring configs.
-Directory `copy` and `symlink-each` footprints are also checked against nested
-dotfile declarations. Disjoint leaves may share directories, but two entries
-cannot own the same leaf or place a file where another entry needs a directory.
-
-Other configuration such as tools, tasks, packages, hooks, and repos is not
-collected from these roots. Use their existing explicit workflows when those
-resources need aggregate behavior.
-
-Use `mise bootstrap config-roots` to inspect the active non-composed bootstrap
-declarations before running those workflows:
-
-```sh
-mise bootstrap config-roots
-mise bootstrap config-roots --json
-```
-
-The command reports package, repo, account, and hook declarations separately
-for every matched configuration root. JSON output includes the declaring config
-and its active configuration environment. Counts describe active TOML entries;
-the command does not inspect the host, resolve resource state, or run bootstrap
-hooks.
-

content.text:
That comment is strong, and it makes me less certain that removing `config_roots` wholesale is the right boundary.

It establishes two things:

- This is real production use—40+ roots—not a speculative request.
- The feature is creating exactly the expansion pressure we’re worried about: composition led to inventory, which immediately led to fan-out execution and playbook semantics.

Their proposed fan-out is nevertheless well designed. It is explicit, deterministic iteration rather than ambiguous merging, and they correctly avoid implicit execution and hook semantics. If mise wants to become a machine orchestrator, this is a reasonable next step.

But your objection was that bootstrap should be global/system-scoped. Their dotfiles setup may already satisfy that principle: a global machine configuration can still be modular. That suggests the actual mistake might be allowing bootstrap to derive from arbitrary project configuration—not necessarily allowing a global bootstrap config to reference modular roots.

I would distinguish:

- Scope: bootstrap must be owned by global/system configuration.
- Modularity: global/system bootstrap may still need components.
- Orchestration: mise should probably decline per-root imperative fan-out.

So I’d reconsider PR #13010 before merging. A more precise direction may be to restrict bootstrap composition to roots selected by global/system config, rather than remove `config_roots` entirely. If you still want full removal, this comment deserves a direct acknowledgment and a concrete migration path; “move everything into one global file” is a meaningful regression for this user.
i don't have time to work on this and consider the drawbacks, it needs to stay deprecated, users should not use it at all

Agreed. In that case, the production usage is a reason to deprecate promptly, not a reason to inherit an expanding maintenance commitment.

The comment demonstrates that `config_roots` is already pulling bootstrap toward orchestration, fan-out, hook scoping, and cross-root lifecycle guarantees. Those are substantial design obligations, and leaving the feature publicly endorsed implicitly commits mise to resolving them.

PR #13010 has the correct posture:

- Stop advertising it.
- Warn all existing users immediately.
- Provide six months to unwind usage.
- Avoid suggesting a successor before the design is understood.
- Decline further expansion during the deprecation window.

Users can keep their current loops temporarily, but should migrate bootstrap state into global/system configuration rather than build more infrastructure around `config_roots`.

I’ll reply directly and clearly: acknowledge the real production use, explain that the expanding orchestration contract is why the feature remains deprecated, and avoid implying that a replacement is planned.
